claims.text: Catalytic activity in transition-metal catalysts is governed primarily by the d-electron occupancy of the metal center.
Catalytic selectivity in transition-metal catalysts is governed primarily by the d-electron occupancy of the metal center.
The d-electron occupancy of a metal center modulates the binding energies of key reaction intermediates.
Changing ligand electron-donating or electron-withdrawing character alters the d-electron occupancy of the metal center.
Electron-donating ligands increase d-electron occupancy at the metal center.
Increasing d-electron occupancy can weaken adsorption of reaction intermediates.
Electron-withdrawing ligands decrease d-electron occupancy at the metal center.
Decreasing d-electron occupancy leads to stronger binding of reaction intermediates.
An intermediate d-electron occupancy produces balanced Sabatier-type binding of catalytic intermediates.
Balanced intermediate binding at an intermediate d-electron occupancy maximizes catalytic activity and selectivity.
Catalysts having an intermediate d-electron occupancy will have higher catalytic activity and selectivity than the unmodified-ligand baseline.
Catalysts made too electron-rich will perform less effectively because intermediates bind too weakly.
Catalysts made too electron-poor will perform less effectively because intermediates bind too strongly.
The proposed relationship should hold when ligand electronic effects dominate catalyst performance.
Support effects, nanoparticle morphology, or mass transport can overwhelm ligand-electronic effects on intermediate binding and catalyst performance.
Trends between d-electron occupancy and intermediate binding energies are well established.
The optimal d-electron occupancy range may vary with reaction type and metal identity.
